title: How do you keep an AI-made art style consistent across a whole roster?
author: Conscious-Season-607
selftext:
Hobby dev here, making a game with mostly AI-generated art. With a handful of characters it was easy, but as the roster grows (heroes, enemies, backdrops, UI) the style keeps drifting from one batch to the next.

1. What do you use to hold a style steady: reference images, a fixed prompt, a trained style, or editing each result by hand?
2. When the style drifts, do you regenerate the older art to match, or fix the new art?
3. How do you keep characters on-model across different poses and animations?
4. Have players reacted to the AI disclosure on your pages, and did it change your numbers?

replies.author: _Dingaloo
replies.body:
You need a centralized workflow. For your art, you need to create your first few assets across whatever (world, character, UI) and then provide those examples (both text and visual examples) in a directory that a agents file points to.

Then every single time you tell the system "make image like this" it should read that file and check the references. Then it'll be more likely to keep it in that design.

But of course you still have to review and make a judgement call on every single generation

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
I experimented with a single reference sheet showing a wide variety of asset types and a material pallet and a description of the style. Then feed both those two into an image generator and a description of the asset you want to specifically make next and have it make an asset sheet. Feed the asset sheet into your image to 3D tool of choice have it retopo, and maybe have AI do any cleanup in blender.

The problem is coherence is very hard. Every asset uses its own textures instead of pulling from a set of quality consistent PBR materials, so there will be subtle differences in how light hits things and optimization will be hard too. For these reasons I’ve abandoned this technique and I’m building a procedural generator that can build all of the assets my game needs from a generator framework and shared set of high quality materials. But this is way more work and quite challenging to build. I happen to find procedural gen very fun so I prefer this route.

comments.author: Elegant_Bonbon
comments.body:
You'll need to define your style system and edit a lot by hand.

AI absolutely sucks at animation.  Try to make rigged models for animation and then adjust animations by hand. Blender for 3D, Spine/Live2D for 2D, Aseprite for pixel all have rigging systems or plugins available.

replies.body: For 2D you can just do videos cut into frames, it generally works well

comments.author: SassyTextDev
comments.body:
What kind of game are you making? I ask because I'm not sure how much this will apply to what you're doing, but...

Checkout \`Black Forest Labs FLUX prompting guide github\`. They published an entire repo of markdown talking about how to get the most out of a prompt, but it applies to more than just their lineup of models.

I've been using gpt2.5-flare for a personal project. Wouldn't suggest for highest quality art, I'm using it because latency and cost are a concern. I'm building a kind of AI driven VN TTRPG... thing, so I need the GM to be able to create a character and then **get that image within 10 seconds**. I've found the FLUX prompt guide mostly applies.

For consistency, I run edits off the art. And I stick to a few styles I found AI can do consistently well. Watercolors, graphite pencil sketch, etc.

comments.author: Previous-Tackle-759
comments.body:
One thing from your reply jumps out: Pinterest. A board of references from twenty different artists is twenty styles, and the model averages them differently every time. That alone can explain the drift.

What worked for me with Nano Banana specifically:

* **Describe the style in plain words, not with reference images.** With images it tends to collapse into copying one picture. Concrete words, no metaphors: "flat colors, thick dark outline, 3 shades per color", not "cozy fantasy vibe".
* **Recolor afterwards with a script.** Fix a palette of 16 to 32 colors and map every generated image to it. Claude can write that script in a few minutes, no strong hardware needed. Half of the drift is color, and this kills it completely.
* **Generate in sheets, judge side by side.** Drift is invisible on one image and obvious on twelve.
* **For poses, edit the master instead of generating new.** Once a character is right, every new pose is an edit of that image, never a fresh generation.

comments.author: Ill-Ant-9489
comments.body:
The durable fix for the batch to batch drift is a trained style LoRA rather than refs or a prompt. You train once on 20 to 40 images that already share the look, then every new asset inherits the style whatever the subject, which a Pinterest board can never do since it averages twenty artists differently each run (the point above about that is spot on). That is what I build tooling around, a Style dataset workflow in https://github.com/perfectgf/lora-dataset-studio.

On the hardware worry, a style LoRA is lighter than you'd think. Z-Image wants about 12 images and the least VRAM of the families, or you rent a GPU for one run. Once it exists you regenerate the older assets through it instead of touching up each one. Which base are you leaning toward for the final art?
